Time Series 4: Vector Autoregressions and Cointegration¶

Several series observed together can influence each other. A vector autoregression (VAR) models each series by the past of all of them; impulse responses and variance decompositions then describe how a shock travels through the system, and Granger tests ask whether one series helps predict another. When the series have unit roots but share a long-run relation, the error-correction form (VECM) and Johansen’s test describe that relation. After this chapter you can fit and select a VAR, trace shocks through it, test for predictive content, and find and estimate cointegrating relations.

Every program is complete and its output is the output of that program.

The VAR¶

For a k-dimensional series y_t the VAR(p) is

y_t = c + A₁ y_{t−1} + … + A_p y_{t−p} + e_t, Cov(e_t) = Σ.

Var::fit_mle(y, VarOptions) takes y as an n × k matrix (one column per series) and fits it by least squares, which is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate. VarOptions: lag_order (p, default 1), include_intercept (true), include_trend (false), ridge (0) and pinv_rcond. A second overload, fit_mle(y, x, options), adds exogenous regressors x.

VarFit holds constant (k), ar (p × k × k), covariance (k × k, the maximum-likelihood estimate: the residual cross-products divided by the number of fitted rows sample_size = n − p) and, with exogenous variables, beta. Layout: ar[l][j][i] is the coefficient of series j at lag l + 1 in the equation of series i, so row j of each matrix lists the effects of series j on all series. The same row-vector convention is used by irf and fevd below: the first index after the step is the shock, the last the response.

Methods: infer(y) (residuals), loglik(y), loglik_per_obs(y), forecast(h, y) (an h × k matrix of point forecasts), simulate(n, cfg, seed), irf, fevd and granger_test.

Impulse responses and variance decompositions¶

Write the VAR as an infinite moving average y_t = Σ Ψ_s e_{t−s}. The orthogonalised responses use the Cholesky factor P of Σ (so Σ = P P') to get uncorrelated shocks: the response of the system s steps after a one-standard-deviation shock to series j is the j-th column of Ψ_s P. The first series is thereby treated as not reacting to the others in the same period, so the order of the columns of y matters. The generalised responses (IrfMethod::Generalized) instead shock series j alone and let the other series respond through the correlation in Σ (Ψ_s Σ e_j / √σ_jj); they do not depend on the ordering.

The forecast-error variance decomposition fevd gives, for each series and horizon, the fraction of its forecast-error variance due to each shock. For the generalised method the shares are normalised to add up to one for each series.

Granger causality¶

Series j does not Granger-cause series i when the lags of j have zero coefficients in the equation of i. granger_test(y, GrangerOptions) tests this by the Wald statistic (GrangerStat::ChiSquare, referred to a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom per restricted coefficient) or its F form (referred to F(dof1, dof2) with dof2 the residual degrees of freedom of the equation). type selects the tests: every ordered pair (LeaveOneOut, the default; cause and effect index lists restrict it), each effect against all other series together (ExcludeAll), or the series in cause jointly against each series in effect (BlockWise). A joint test reports -1 in the cause field.

Cointegration¶

Series that each have a unit root can still have a stationary linear combination: they are cointegrated. Their error-correction form is

Δy_t = c + y_{t−1} β α’ + Γ₁ Δy_{t−1} + … + Γ_{p−1} Δy_{t−p+1} + e_t,

where the columns of β (k × r) are the cointegrating vectors (y_{t−1} β is stationary), the columns of α (k × r) say how each series adjusts to a deviation, and r, the rank, is the number of independent relations. Johansen’s procedure finds r from the squared canonical correlations between the changes and the lagged levels, after the constant, the trend and the lagged differences have been removed.

johansen_test(y, JohansenOptions) tests the sequence “rank ≤ r” for r = 0, 1, …, either by the trace statistic (against any larger rank) or the maximum-eigenvalue statistic (against rank r + 1). Neither follows a chi-squared law; the limiting distributions are non-standard functionals of Brownian motion and depend on the deterministic terms and on the number m = k − r of series still tested. The library compares the statistics with simulated limiting distributions for three specifications (selected by the options): no deterministic terms, an unrestricted constant (include_intercept), and an unrestricted constant with a trend (include_trend), for up to 12 series. selected_rank is the first r that is not rejected.

Vecm::fit_mle(y, VecmOptions) fits the error-correction model for a given rank (negative: chosen by the trace test at level alpha). Its beta is normalised so that its leading r × r block is the identity, its alpha holds the adjustment loadings, and impact = β α'. For 0 < rank < k the estimate is Johansen’s maximum-likelihood one, for rank = k it is least squares, and for rank = 0 it is the VAR in differences. In both functions lag_order is the order p of the VAR in levels.

Checklist¶

  1. Use levels for the VAR only if the series are stationary; otherwise difference them or test for cointegration first (Chapter 1: ADF and KPSS).

  2. Choose the lag order by Akaike’s or Schwarz’s criterion from loglik, with k (k p + 1) parameters.

  3. Order the series before orthogonalising impulse responses; use the generalised version when there is no natural order.

  4. For a cointegration test pass the levels, state the deterministic terms honestly, and read selected_rank from the sequence of tests.

  5. Fit the VECM with the chosen rank; read beta as the long-run relation and alpha as the speed of adjustment.
